pr.title: Actually use the inferred `ClosureKind` from signature inference in coroutine-closures
pr.author: compiler-errors

processing.reason:
The historical defect in PR #123350 is not a value-producing miscompilation: the incorrect `ByMoveBody` early-return (`coroutine_kind == FnOnce` instead of `InstanceDef::CoroutineKindShim`) leaves the inner coroutine borrowing an upvar from a consumed `FnOnce` coroutine-closure. The PR's own evidence says this “will always result in a borrowck error” (E0597/`x does not live long enough`); the corresponding `.stderr` files are added by patch 1 and deleted by patch 2. The valid final behavior is simply that the previously rejected `force_fnonce(async move || println!(\"{x:?}\"))` cases compile and print `Hello(6)`/`Hello(7)`.

Consequently there is no source-grounded original/transformed function pair that both pass Miri and compute different values. A by-move capture and an inner borrow of the same immutable upvar read the same value, so making both versions executable would produce identical output. Constructing a difference would require either (a) unsafe/dangling access or leaking the parent so the borrow outlives it, or (b) mutating the captured value after the move/borrow. Those are not the historical transformation: the former is UB or an artificial lifetime workaround, and the latter is the post-copy-overwrite conflation explicitly excluded by the preconditions/pitfalls. Encoding such behavior would manufacture an unrelated rewrite merely to force a runtime divergence. Therefore no valid counterexample pair can be validated for this borrowck-only fix.

analysis.summary: The coroutine by-move body transformation must not assume that an `FnOnce` coroutine kind means all upvars were already moved. For async closures whose kind is restricted to `FnOnce` by signature inference, an inner coroutine can still borrow an upvar from its parent closure, causing E0597. The fix detects `FnOnce` coroutine-closures and forces the inner coroutine capture clause to match the parent `move` closure, and changes the by-move-body skip condition to the `CoroutineKindShim` rather than `FnOnce`.
analysis.originalLogic: The original by-move-body logic returned early when the coroutine kind resolved to `FnOnce`: "We don't need to generate a by-move coroutine if the kind of the coroutine is already `FnOnce` -- that means that any upvars that the closure consumes have already been taken by-value." It then computed `coroutine_kind` and only inserted by-ref fields when the coroutine captured by ref and the parent captured by value.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect transformation equated `coroutine_kind == ty::ClosureKind::FnOnce` with "all upvars already taken by-value" and skipped the by-move rewriting. But the PR states: "The outer closure captures `x` by move, but the inner coroutine still immutably borrows `x` from the outer closure." Because "the signature of `AsyncFnOnce::call_once` doesn't have a borrowed lifetime", this led to borrowck errors. Patch 2 corrected this by skipping only for `body.source.instance, ty::InstanceDef::CoroutineKindShim { .. }` and by adding an assertion that "`FnOnce` coroutine-closures return coroutines that capture from their body; it will always result in a borrowck error!" It also forced the inner coroutine to be `move` when the parent coroutine-closure was inferred `FnOnce`: "we force the inner coroutine to also be `move`."
analysis.inputDomain: Async closures (coroutine-closures desugared with `hir::CoroutineSource::Closure`) passed where the expected parameter type forces the closure kind, e.g. `fn force_fnonce<T>(f: impl async FnOnce() -> T) -> impl async FnOnce() -> T`. Include `async move` closures and non-`move` `async` closures capturing both owned values and references, where the inner coroutine only reads the captured value.
analysis.trigger: An `async move` closure constrained to `ClosureKind::FnOnce` by signature inference, whose inner coroutine captures an upvar by reference instead of by move. The PR describes forcing a closure via `fn(x: impl async FnOnce())` as "artificially restricting the kind of the async closure to `ClosureKind::FnOnce`."
preconditions: The parent is an async closure desugared from a closure (`hir::CoroutineKind::Desugared(_, hir::CoroutineSource::Closure)`).
The parent closure kind was inferred or constrained to `ty::ClosureKind::FnOnce`, not merely the inner coroutine's kind.
The inner coroutine may capture an upvar by reference from the parent, especially when the body only reads the upvar.
The parent coroutine-closure is `move`; the PR notes that otherwise the closure itself borrows from the outer environment and there are no self-borrows.
pitfalls: `FnOnce` coroutine kind alone does not prove that upvars were consumed by value; signature inference can make the kind more restrictive than the inner coroutine's captures.
Do not conflate borrowck restrictions with post-copy overwrites; the failing case here is a self-borrow from the parent coroutine-closure, not an overwrite after a copy.

`AsyncFnOnce::call_once` has no borrowed lifetime, so an async `FnOnce` coroutine cannot borrow from its parent closure: "This would lead to an impossible to satisfy situation, since `AsyncFnOnce`" coroutine bodies cannot borrow from their parent closure.

The correct skip condition for by-move body generation is `CoroutineKindShim`, not `FnOnce`: "We don't need to generate a by-move coroutine if the kind of the coroutine is" already `FnOnce` is not a valid reason to skip the rewrite.
Forcing the inner coroutine to `move` is described as safe because with an `async FnOnce()` that is `move`, "there's no reason to ever borrow anything, so `move` isn't artificially restrictive."
analysis.testStrategy: Use the paired UI and Miri regression tests `tests/ui/async-await/async-closures/captures.rs` and `src/tools/miri/tests/pass/async-closure-captures.rs`, which are explicitly kept in sync. Add a `force_fnonce` helper and cover both owned and reference captures under two cases: "// Capture something with `move`, but infer to `AsyncFnOnce`" and "// Capture something by-ref, but infer to `AsyncFnOnce`". In the final patch, the UI test is restored to `//@ run-pass` with `//@ check-run-results`, the E0597 `.stderr` expectation is deleted, and the expected output gains `Hello(6)` through `Hello(9)`. Also exercise `wrong-fn-kind.rs`: the mutation through an `async Fn`-bound closure now produces `cannot borrow `x` as mutable, as it is a captured variable in a `Fn` closure` (E0596) rather than only the old E0525 diagnostic. These are patch expectations; no compiler was built or executed.
evidence: Actually use the inferred `ClosureKind` from signature inference in coroutine-closures
A follow-up to https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/123349, which fixes another subtle bug: We were not taking into account the async closure kind we infer during closure signature inference.

When I pass a closure directly to an arg like `fn(x: impl async FnOnce())`, that should have the side-effect of artificially restricting the kind of the async closure to `ClosureKind::FnOnce`. We weren't doing this -- that's a quick fix; however, it uncovers a second, more subtle bug with the way that `move`, async closures, and `FnOnce` interact.

The outer closure captures `x` by move, but the inner coroutine still immutably borrows `x` from the outer closure. Since we've forced the closure to by `async FnOnce()`, we can't actually *do* a self borrow, since the signature of `AsyncFnOnce::call_once` doesn't have a borrowed lifetime. This means that all `async move` closures that are constrained to `FnOnce` will fail borrowck.

We can fix that by detecting this case specifically, and making the *inner* async closure `move` as well. This is always beneficial to closure analysis, since if we have an `async FnOnce()` that's `move`, there's no reason to ever borrow anything, so `move` isn't artificially restrictive.
